title: Cooperative exploration and target search
role: Graduate Researcher · Advisor: Dr. Srikanth Saripalli
summary: Built frontier exploration on a physical Jackal and extended the pipeline to coordinated mapping, task allocation and target search with one Husky and two Jackals in simulation.
challenge: A robot exploring an unknown environment must map free space, choose reachable frontiers and navigate safely. With multiple robots, the team must also divide work as the map changes. I first developed and demonstrated the pipeline on a Jackal, then extended its mapping, allocation and search components to a simulated Husky and two Jackals.
contributions: Jackal exploration

Deployed a VLP-16 equipped Jackal J100 with LiDAR mapping, Wavefront Frontier Detection and nearest eligible frontier selection. Used Nav2 Smac A* and DWB to navigate in the lab, with heading alignment and checks for unreachable or failed goals.
Localization and safe navigation

Used wheel encoder odometry fused with IMU measurements by an EKF for local motion estimates. AMCL estimates pose from LiDAR against an existing map; SLAM Toolbox supports map building in the exploration workflow. Added a costmap layer to reject high cost cells and a DWB critic to slow forward motion near obstacles.
Cooperative exploration

Built a shared occupancy map and used balanced Hungarian assignment to distribute detected frontiers among one Husky and two Jackals in simulation. Each robot receives a distance ordered goal queue, navigates with its own Nav2 stack and contributes observations that trigger updated assignments.
Visual target search

Connected Smac A* and MPPI navigation with pretrained YOLO inference on the simulated robots’ camera streams. Required detections across successive frames before reporting the target and ending the search.
outcome: Demonstrated autonomous frontier exploration on a physical Jackal. In simulation, the Husky and two Jackals share map updates, divide frontier tasks and run visual target detection. The linked video shows the Jackal hardware demonstration.
imageAlt: Cooperative exploration workflow: AMCL provides localization within an existing map, supported by EKF fusion of wheel encoder odometry and IMU measurements. Shared LiDAR mapping, wavefront frontier detection, Hungarian task allocation and A* planning with MPPI control support exploration. Camera-based target detection runs alongside exploration.
imageCaption: Scaling exploration to a robot team: shared observations update the map, Hungarian assignment distributes frontier tasks, and each robot executes its own navigation goals.
videoDescription: The video shows the single-Jackal hardware implementation that supports the current extension to cooperative multi-robot exploration.

researchScope.overview: Investigating how a heterogeneous robot team can efficiently explore an unknown outdoor environment through capability-based task allocation. Exploration tasks are assigned according to each robot’s mobility and sensing capabilities and the access requirements of unexplored regions.

title: Automated Perception and Planning for Rural Roads
eyebrow: Autonomous Vehicles for All · Perception & planning
role: Graduate Research Assistant · Advisor: Dr. Reza Langari
status: Vehicle-oriented ROS 2 implementation · recorded-data and simulation workflows
summary: Developed ROS 2 road perception and Frenet trajectory planning for marked and unmarked rural roads.
imageAlt: Annotated AVA research vehicle with its sensor locations
imageCaption: AVA research vehicle and sensor layout. Project scope: perception and motion planning.
challenge: On rural roads, lane markings can be faint or absent, making it difficult to define a safe driving corridor. I developed a perception and planning workflow to estimate road boundaries and generate local trajectories. I also built a separate OpenStreetMap driver assistance prototype and studied visual feature redundancy.
contributions: Road perception

Integrated CLRerNet, SAM2 and SphereFormer to detect lane markings and segment road surfaces from camera and LiDAR data. Projected LiDAR into the camera frame and extracted left and right road edges from segmented point clouds.
Object association and planning

Associated YOLOv9 camera detections with synchronized LiDAR and radar observations. Generated Frenet trajectories using lateral quintic and longitudinal quartic polynomials, then selected references by smoothness, duration, offset and speed error.
Related prototypes

Built an OpenStreetMap dashboard that matches recorded odometry to route segments and provides curve, intersection and speed advisories. Separately applied PCA to OpenDriveVLA features from 6,019 nuScenes samples to measure visual representation redundancy.
outcome: Delivered ROS 2 modules for road and object perception and local trajectory references, plus the separate driver assistance prototype. In the PCA study, about ten components retained 80% of scene token variance and 97% of map token variance.

title: Precision Vehicle Tracking and Disturbance Recovery
date: 2024 concept study · 2026 tracking and recovery study
summary: Designed a constrained vehicle tracking controller and evaluated its response to startup error and disturbance in simulation.
challenge: A trajectory controller needs to track a changing path while respecting limits on steering, acceleration and speed. I tested a reference scheduled predictive controller against a nonlinear vehicle model on variable speed and disturbed trajectories.
contributions: Model
Formulated along track, cross track, heading and speed errors against a time indexed reference. Scheduled the prediction model using reference speed and curvature over a 20 step horizon.
Control
Solved a sparse quadratic program with OSQP every 100 ms of simulated time. Constrained steering, acceleration, input changes and speed, applying the first optimized command at each step.
Evaluation

Ran oval, figure eight and disturbed lane change scenarios with a nonlinear kinematic bicycle model. Measured tracking error and recovery, and independently checked command and sampled speed constraints.
outcome: All 1,520 optimization solves succeeded across three simulated scenarios. Position RMSE ranged from 0.289 to 0.396 m, including startup recovery; configured constraint checks passed.
resources: Precision Vehicle Tracking and Disturbance Recovery · theoretical report
sourceNote: Builds on concepts from Mark Misin’s study.

title: Robotic welding automation
role: Graduate Research Assistant · Advisor: Dr. Prabhakar Pagilla
summary: Connected CAD part registration, torch path planning and welder commands in a UR10e welding workflow.
challenge: Automating a weld requires the planned seam in CAD to align with the physical workpiece, and torch motion to stay synchronized with the welding process. I developed a workflow connecting geometry selection, robot planning and execution.
contributions: Registration
Paired measured workpiece points with CAD features to register the part in the robot frame. Used the selected seam to define weld targets, torch orientation and approach and retreat waypoints.
Planning
Interpolated torch poses and used MoveIt to plan and time trajectories for a requested travel speed. Logged joint and reconstructed tool positions to inspect planned motion.
Execution
Integrated PyQt5 and RViz with the UR10e and welder voltage, wire feed and trigger commands. Later connected infrared monitoring to travel speed and arc voltage feedback.
outcome: Demonstrated an integrated CAD to robot welding workflow with motion diagnostics and tool position logging. The infrared feedback work was a later extension.
sourceNote: Technical explanation based on the project report and the pre-closed-loop implementation supplied for review. Report figures document this earlier platform. The later process-feedback extension is described separately; proprietary source code is not distributed.

title: Robot motion and feedback control at MIKO
summary: Developed feedback control and sensor integration for expressive, balancing and interactive robot prototypes at MIKO.
challenge: Interactive robots need repeatable motion and stable responses despite physical mechanisms and noisy sensor inputs. At MIKO, I worked on head articulation, a self balancing mobile platform and speaker directed orientation.
contributions: Head motion
Measured mechanism responses, modeled the head articulation system and developed motion planning and robust feedback control for expressive joint movement.
Balance
Integrated sensors on a self balancing robot, tuned feedback controllers and evaluated stability and movement on the physical prototype.
Interaction
Converted audio direction of arrival estimates into yaw targets so the robot could turn toward a speaker, and added remote control functionality.
outcome: Tested motion and interaction functions on physical prototypes. The linked demonstration shows a prototype from this work.
sourceNote: The demonstration shows a self-balancing prototype, not a specific commercial MIKO product.

title: Robust control for vehicle platooning
summary: Compared robust spacing and path tracking controllers for a simulated leader and two follower vehicles.
imageAlt: Master's thesis plot of lateral tracking error using super-twisting control
imageCaption: Lateral tracking error with super-twisting control, reproduced from the master's thesis.
challenge: A vehicle platoon must preserve longitudinal spacing and follow the leader’s path without excessive control effort. My master’s thesis compared nonlinear controllers on a three vehicle simulation to examine tracking, convergence and actuation cost.
contributions: System model
Modeled the platoon with nonlinear bicycle dynamics in MATLAB/Simulink at a reference speed of 8 m/s. Used a Luenberger observer to estimate yaw rate from lateral velocity.
Controller comparison
Implemented PID, conventional sliding mode, the thesis’s power rate exponential reaching law (PREL), and second order super twisting for longitudinal and lateral control.
Evaluation
Compared absolute, squared and time weighted tracking errors together with control effort, so lower tracking error could be assessed alongside actuation demand.
outcome: PREL had the lowest error indices in the documented simulations. Super twisting gave lateral convergence without overshoot and the lowest longitudinal control energy metric. Related work appeared at ACODS 2022.

title: A robot swarm searching for light
summary: Used Particle Swarm Optimization to guide three LEGO NXT robots toward a light source in a physical arena.
imageAlt: LEGO NXT robot carrying an ArUco tracking marker
imageCaption: LEGO NXT platform with an ArUco marker for overhead tracking.
challenge: A team searching for a light source needs to combine each robot’s observations with information shared by the group. This project tested whether a particle swarm search could drive real robots toward the brightest area.
contributions: Search
Developed particle swarm updates in MATLAB and implemented the robot workflow in Python. Combined each robot’s best light reading with the team’s best reading to set new motion targets.
Localization
Tracked robot positions with an overhead camera and ArUco markers, then sent motion commands through a central Bluetooth controller.
Hardware trials
Connected light sensing, waypoint following and ultrasonic obstacle avoidance on three LEGO NXT robots and evaluated convergence in the arena.
outcome: The robots converged toward the brightest region; one documented trial took 11 iterations. The related paper won a Best Paper Award at ICECA 2019.

title: EKF-SLAM and embedded robot navigation
eyebrow: IIT Bombay internship · Estimation & embedded control
role: Summer intern · Joint project with Alden J. Joseph
summary: Studied EKF based robot and landmark estimation in MATLAB and separately programmed obstacle avoiding navigation on a SPARK-V robot.
imageAlt: MATLAB EKF-SLAM simulation showing a robot path and landmark estimates
imageCaption: EKF-SLAM simulation from the internship report, showing a waypoint route and estimated landmarks.
challenge: A moving robot must estimate where it is while identifying landmarks from noisy measurements. During an internship, I studied joint estimation in a MATLAB EKF-SLAM simulator and separately implemented encoder assisted navigation on embedded hardware.
contributions: EKF-SLAM
Adapted a credited MATLAB simulator to estimate robot pose and landmark positions with prediction and measurement updates and Jacobian based covariance propagation.
Data association
Matched range and bearing observations to landmarks using Mahalanobis gating, then examined how repeated observations changed map uncertainty.
Embedded navigation
Programmed ultrasonic obstacle avoidance and encoder feedback in Embedded C for a SPARK-V robot with an ATmega16 controller.
outcome: Reobserving landmarks reduced estimated map uncertainty in simulation. The separate SPARK-V implementation demonstrated room traversal with obstacle avoidance.

title: Needle-tip tracking with Kalman filtering
summary: Combined ultrasound image processing and Kalman filtering to track a needle tip against electromagnetic reference measurements.
challenge: Ultrasound speckle and unrelated edges can make needle tip localization unstable from frame to frame. I built a LabVIEW tracking pipeline and compared its position estimates with an independent electromagnetic reference.
contributions: Image measurements
Used background subtraction and edge detection in a region of interest, then fit a needle line with RANSAC to reject unrelated image edges.
State estimation
Used a four state Kalman filter to combine predicted motion with image measurements across frames.
Validation
Tested insertion in artificial and biological tissue to depths of 6.5 cm, comparing the combined estimator with vision only tracking using an NDI Aurora reference.
outcome: Position RMSE decreased from 0.79 to 0.03 cm in artificial tissue and from 0.84 to 0.21 cm in biological tissue compared with vision only tracking under the reported experimental conditions.
